That is, there is an immense difference between this relation and the other relations discussed. Words are used for general meanings even when the levels they cover differ greatly. — س ره

Put another way, after carefully considering essence apart from every kind of existence, essence is not “existence” in the strict, primary sense, even though in broader usage it is called existence. — ه ره

Some copies say “the concept of existence”; the meaning is the same. The abstract noun “existence” means existence considered on its own, while “existent” means existence without restriction. The difference is like that between a feature and an adjective made from it: “whiteness” considered on its own is not predicated of a subject, while “white” is; they differ only in form, just as unrestricted whiteness and “white” differ in how they are used in a sentence. The commentator then says that the different meanings under discussion may be features either in reality or in thought. Existence as a separate abstract noun cannot be a feature in reality or thought. Once essence is considered in itself, it is not described by that isolated idea of existence, but by “existent” or by existence in its ordinary meaning. The Sayyid does not hold that the underlying feature must literally inhere in the subject for an adjective to apply. The other two meanings may be features in thought, but not in reality. — س ره

“Far apart are dust and the Lord of lords, water and a mirage, darkness and light!” The author says that essence disappears into existence and that, in reality, essence is its own being. The Sayyid says instead that existence disappears into essence and that essence is its being. Both reject a real division between the two. But what makes it true to predicate the idea of existence of an essence? The Sayyid does not say that existence is a feature inhering in essence, either outside the mind or in thought, nor that it is connected to essence by some other relation. If so, there would be no difference between a true and a false statement. He does say that things exist by being united with the idea of existence, as he explains later. But what makes that union true? It must already be established. — س ره
This conflicts with what the same author says later: no one disputes that essence and existence differ in thought, not in the outside world. Consider this carefully. — س ره

One can reply that to doubt something is to picture it as an open question. What exists outside the mind cannot be pictured in that way; whatever we picture is an abstract idea. At most, this proves a difference in thought, not in reality. It therefore defeats Suhrawardi's claim that existence itself needs another existence and also the Aristotelian claim that existence is added to essence in the outside world. It does not, however, defeat the claim that a possible thing's existence is added to its essence in thought, which both sides accept. The commentator also suggests another reading: the author may mean that his answer to Suhrawardi's argument for existence being fundamental also applies to the Aristotelian proof that existence is added to essence in thought. A note the author wrote while discussing this argument in The Philosophy of Illumination supports that reading: the same response works whether the argument is used against the Aristotelian proof that existence is added to essence or as proof that nothing exists whose essence is existence itself. — س ره

The cases where existence differs from substance and quality include God's existence; the cases where substance or quality differs from existence include the four kinds of quality. You might object that whenever the four qualities exist, existence exists too, since an essence cannot be established without existence. If you consider only what those natures are in themselves, they count as qualities in the strict, defining sense, not as actual instances of the general kind “quality”; quality itself is not an instance of itself. For them to count as actual qualities that are not instances of existence, there would have to be a real case of quality that is not a real case of existence. Yet, as al-Lahiji says, the cases that distinguish two concepts must differ in their realities, not merely in how we think about them. We reply that only on your view—where individuality is existence—is the essence of quality an instance of existence. The Shaykh holds that a thing becomes an individual through its own essence after it is made, even if that view is mistaken in reality. If existences are real, they are like accidents that belong to subjects after those subjects are already complete in their own natures. On his view, the particular existence of each quality would be like a particular quality belonging to another particular quality, as an accident belongs to its subject. — س ره
Careful thought shows that this is a proof, not merely an argument designed to corner the other side. — س ره

That is, real existence lies outside both essence and the general idea of existence, and differs from them as a standing person differs from a shadow, or a shadow from the person who casts it. Yet it is united with essence as something not yet fully determined is united with what makes it definite. “Accidental,” in the sense of a feature predicated of things from outside their definition, applies to the general concept of existence, as the author says below. — س ره

The claim that the reality of light is not universal or particular applies to a meaning broad enough to include God, immaterial beings, and sensory light. But visible light, which the eye perceives, is certainly one of the kinds of things that have an essence and can be considered universal or particular, like anything else. — ط مد

Do not take “unfolding” or “descent” to mean literal movement from one place to another. For something to flow from a source does not mean that the source leaves its place or loses any of its levels. It means that the source casts a shadow or reflection: something proceeds from it without reducing its perfection. If that manifestation returns to it, it adds nothing to its perfection. The true Giver has a reality in which His manifestations have no share, while none of them has any reality apart from Him. A familiar example is light reflected from the sun to the moon, from the moon to a mirror, from the mirror to water, and from the water to a wall. — س ره

The author pictures spiritual light and darkness as two cones pointing in opposite directions. The cone of light has its broad base in the world of intellect and its tip in the material world; the cone of darkness has its tip in the world of intellect and its broad base in the material world. — س ره

It is called existence as a predicate because it is what we affirm in simple statements such as “X exists.” In the predicate position, what matters is the concept; what that concept refers to is what is affirmed of all actual things and even of illusory essences. Another explanation is that the mind knows how things are connected to the reality named by this concept and can affirm that connection. But as for what that reality is in itself, none knows it except He. — س ره

Since the simple statement “X exists” comes before the compound statement “X is such-and-such,” we are now concerned with existence as what makes something real, not with its unity, which already presupposes that reality. The view that all existences depend on God is the special understanding of divine oneness. The fitting religious way to express this is that all existences are wholly dependent and needy before the One who is utterly self-sufficient: “You are the ones in need of God, while God is the Self-Sufficient.” True monotheists mean nothing else by their oneness. Woe to a doctrine of oneness that means something other than this, and to a claim of singleness that misses this point. — س ره

“Being” expresses a relation. When real existence is attributed to itself, the relation is like a thing's relation to itself. When being is attributed to an essence, the relation is like a thing's relation to something else. — ن ره

The Dawning Lights by al-Lahiji suggests that the first view belongs to al-Dawani. The meticulous Sayyid, however, says that existence is prior to essence because it is more truly entitled to reality. Perhaps, then, the author means al-Dawani by “some careful scholars.” I do not have their books at hand to check. — س ره

This does not work for a statement in which subject and predicate mean exactly the same thing, because such a statement says they are one in meaning. But in The Book of Insights, the author argues that without the primacy of existence we could not make ordinary true statements, only definitions. Here he goes further: without it, no statement would be possible at all. Even in a statement where subject and predicate are one in meaning, what makes them one is existence—not existence as something contained in a thing, but existence as the link between them. The earlier argument in The Book of Insights is a concession to a less exact way of speaking. — س ره

The author calls the human being's union with existence a unity in reality, although existence is an added feature of the human essence when we consider the human being's thinghood. This follows from its union with the human being's actual existence, which is itself the reality of the human being. — س ره

This may sound as though the real existence of whiteness were the very existence attributed to the human being. That cannot be right, since one existence would then have to be both a substance and an accident. The answer is that when the existence of whiteness is considered without restriction, it is one level of the human being's existence: it belongs to the human being in its own right, but only indirectly to the idea of whiteness or to “what is white.” — س ره
In the first example, one of the two is an idea drawn from reality; in the remaining examples, the other—or both—are. — س ره

The author restates his point as a choice between two possibilities: two fully real things cannot be one, but a mental idea and a real thing can be united. Otherwise, once we establish that what makes them one is real and that one or both sides is only an idea drawn from reality, there is no remaining question to settle. — س ره

Calling real existence a “concept” means that some aspect of it appears in the mind. A thing's aspect is, in a way, the thing itself, so we can describe the reality through what appears of it—as we speak of a universal nature even though its universality exists only in the mind. Or perhaps “concept” is being used to mean “reality,” as it often is among those who know through direct insight. As the verse says: “All are words, but you are the meaning, you who draw hearts to yourself.” If real existence is said to be shared among essences because they share one general concept, that would be impossible: one concept cannot be drawn from different realities precisely as different. We discussed this when treating the shared meaning of existence. Real existence is shared among essences because their possible features and effects appear through it. Its different levels are shared in one respect, since what makes them alike is also what makes each distinct; in another respect they are distinct, since what makes them distinct is also what they share. Understand this and hold to it. — س ره

There seems to be a copying error here. I think the correct wording is: “Both real existence and the abstract concept of existence are shared among essences.” There is no need for the elaborate explanation offered by Mullā Hādī Sabzawārī.

This points to the realm of existence as a mirror that reveals the realities of things and their states. The words “If existence did not shine within the things that are, and reveal itself through them” point to the reverse as well: things and their realities are mirrors that reveal the reality of existence, its attributes, and its names. This is a profound secret to those who know. — ن ره

People who speak of God's oneness take four positions. (1) They may accept that both existences and existent things are many, while professing God's oneness aloud and holding to it in a general way. Most people are at this level; this is ordinary monotheism. (2) They may say that both existence and what exists are one. This is the view of some Sufis; it is the most special form of monotheism. (3) They may say that existence is one but existent things are many. This is the position attributed to the spiritual insight of the divine philosophers; it is special monotheism. (4) They may say that existence and what exists are one within their very multiplicity. This is the author's view and the view of the highest mystics; it is the highest form of monotheism. Another classification divides monotheism into oneness of effects, acts, attributes, and essence.

The difference between the author's way and the view attributed to the divine philosophers is this. The author accepts many existences and many existent things, while also affirming unity within that multiplicity. Think of one person standing before many mirrors. The person appears many times, and each reflection has the form of a human being. There are many images, and yet, because each image is only a reflection and has no independent reality, they are one in the very midst of their multiplicity. If you attend to the person who is reflected, the images become ways of seeing that person. If you treat the images as independent things, you lose sight of what they are. The same relation can hold through a hierarchy of levels or across levels that are far apart, as when the same face appears tiny in ice, dimly in muddy water, or clearly in a mirror.

The presence of the one who is reflected is like a thread that strings together the many different images, connects them, gathers what is scattered, and joins opposites. In the same way, when we see existences as dependent manifestations of God—as flashes of His light—they are never wholly separate from His own appearing. But if we take them as independent things, we misunderstand their reality, because dependence belongs to them by their very nature. For the author, existence is one reality with levels that differ in strength and weakness. The very feature that makes the levels different is also what they share, and this confirms their unity: the more fully reality is affirmed and found, the wider its scope and the less it is marked by absence and loss. This is why he calls the multiplicity of existences luminous, while the multiplicity of essences is dark.

Particular contingent existences are real, but they are rays of the sun of reality and pure relations of dependence; they are not separate things that happen to have a relation to God. The author will soon criticize the claim, made in a treatise called al-Zawrāʾ, that the existence of things is a relation to God rather than a relation that itself exists.

By contrast, the other group's view is that real existence is one individual, with no multiplicity in any way, while the many existent things are essences. They exist by being related to real existence, not through distinct contingent existences understood as need and dependence. They allow the derived word “existent” to apply more broadly than something in which the source meaning of the word inheres: it can also apply to what is merely related to that source, and even to the source itself. They say that the realities of things cannot be established by ordinary language, so there is no problem in saying that an essence is “existent” simply because it is related to existence. Arabic usage allows similar words, such as names for someone who sells milk, dates, or iron. They also hold that essences are real; if essences were only ideas drawn from something else, they would have to be drawn from God's existence, since they recognize no other existence.

The author rejects this view for three reasons. First, how can one and the same real existence belong to itself and to other things—making it both a substance and an accident, and both prior and later—when things with the same essence, such as human beings, do not differ in their essence or admit degrees? Second, if the relation to God is a real, illuminating connection, it would itself have to be another existence beyond God's one existence, which this view denies. The relation must therefore be an ordinary relation that depends on both things already existing. But essence is not simply identical with dependence: the essence whose existence we question is not the same as its relation to God. This objection does not apply in the same way to the author's view, because existence cannot be grasped as a concept apart from the realities we encounter; still, such a relation of identity does not fit the other group's view. They treat essences as fully real in themselves, whereas identity through relation can hold only between what is not yet fully determined and what makes it definite—not between two already complete realities, as will be explained later.

Third, if existence is simply what makes things existent, then those relations must themselves be many existences. How, then, can this view count as special monotheism or as belief in one existence? It becomes ordinary monotheism, like the view that both existence and existent things are many. By treating essences as primary realities distinct in their very nature from existence, they end up affirming a second reality alongside existence. So they do not escape a subtle form of associating others with God. May God make us among His sincere servants—indeed, among those made wholly sincere for Him. The author, by contrast, treats what is related to God as existence too. There is nothing in the house but existence.

The first and third objections may seem inconsistent. The first assumes that God's necessary existence is the existence of things; the third assumes that their existences are many mental relations. We can answer that the proponents of this view express it in different ways: sometimes they say that what makes things existent is their relation to God; at other times, they say that Zayd's existence serves as a means of presenting Zayd. One objection addresses the first version and the other the second. Consider this carefully. — س ره

If “thing” means something whose existence is in question—that is, an essence, as in the author's earlier distinction between the familiar names for kinds of thing and the unfamiliar names for kinds of existence—then saying that thinghood and existence go together means that they are realized together. Wherever an essence is realized, its particular existence is realized too, and the two move together. Otherwise, the claim means that they are one in reality. To explain this: as we have seen, existence has a reality of its own. It is one reality that differs in strength and weakness, necessity and possibility, and other ways. Its highest level, complete in every respect and without any deficiency, is the Necessary Existence, which has no essence apart from its existence. Every level below it has a limit and a deficiency. The definition of a human being as a rational animal, for example, tells us about the limits of that person's existence; the definition of an animal as a body that grows and moves by sensation and will tells us about the limits of an animal's existence. A deficiency depends on the existence it limits; it cannot be real without it. This also clarifies a further dispute: does existence become real before essence is established, or does essence become established first? Some people argue that a nonexistent thing must still be a thing because it is necessary for something to be itself, and impossible for it not to be itself. We reply that a thing is itself by its very nature, not because it has existed from eternity. It can fail to be itself when it does not exist, because then there is no thing at all—only nonexistence. This view is extremely weak, unless its supporters mean to defend God's eternal knowledge. But in eternity a nonexistent thing is sheer nothing: it has no disclosure or distinction by which it is known, and it has neither external nor mental existence. Otherwise there would be multiplicity in God's essence and things would be eternal alongside Him. Still, we do not need to say that things have a fixed reality detached from every kind of existence. Their reality follows from God's own existence, as the Sufis hold. — س ره

This argument, and the final point made by the Illuminationist philosopher, rest on the view common among those thinkers: most held that essences are established even in nonexistence and that “states” are also fixed. As al-Kātibī says, they treated being a substance as a state, even though it belongs to an essence whether it exists or not. As Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi says, they explained differences among nonexistent essences by means of states. For them, a state is a feature of a thing that is neither existent nor nonexistent. But under the familiar definition—a feature of something existent that is itself neither existent nor nonexistent—a state would be like the abstract features of existing things. Existence itself would then be a state belonging to something that already exists, not a feature of an essence while it is nonexistent. Otherwise it would not be a feature of something existent. — س ره

The either-or question is meant to force the other side to answer. In their own account, a state is fixed because it is a feature. It cannot be existent, or the features themselves would need further features without end; it cannot be nonexistent either, or the thing would have a feature opposed to its own nature. — س ره

“Thinghood” faces the same problem as possibility. We call thinghood fixed because it is a feature. If they refuse to let a thing be described by what is fixed of it, then they cannot call it possible. If they accept that conclusion, nothing is possible, even though they have called it possible. — س ره

They may say either that God is the agent in an absolute sense, or that His existence is identical with His essence. The first claim is contradicted by names such as “the worshipped” and “the praised,” which are passive forms and are still applied to Him. The second is contradicted by all the beautiful names. Scripture also uses the word “existent” of Him, as in the prayer: “I call upon You, O You who are present everywhere; perhaps You will hear my cry.” — س ره

The author's wording in this chapter is compressed and not entirely clear. A later chapter will explain the difference between linking existence and dependent existence, clarify what is meant by a “state,” and set out the important principles that follow from these distinctions. We will return to them there. — ط ره

The three modalities—necessity, possibility, and impossibility—are features of this kind of existence. To sum up: there is linking existence and existence stated as a predicate. Linking existence means that one thing is affirmed of another. It is what we mean in “whiteness is present in the body” or “the body is white”; even if we omit the linking word, the connection is still there. This link is not an idea that stands on its own. It is like a grammatical particle: we cannot make it a separate subject of a statement without changing it into existence stated as a predicate. It links parts of affirmative statements; a negative statement denies the link. It is also different from the judgment that subject and predicate are one, which occurs in every statement. This kind of linking existence occurs in affirmative statements with a subject and predicate, but not in simple statements such as “X exists.” The author calls it linking existence, following his teacher in The Clear Horizon, to avoid confusing it with dependent existence. Al-Lahiji, in one of his books, called the existence of accidents in their subjects “linking existence” and confused the two. Existence stated as a predicate, by contrast, means that something exists in itself, as in a complete statement such as “X exists.” A thing may exist in itself and for itself, as an intellect or body does; or it may exist in itself but not for itself, as an accident does when it depends on a subject. The first is existence in itself; it is either through itself, as God's existence is, or through another, as the existence of substances that do not inhere in a subject. — س ره
That is, they agree in their nature, since existence has no species and is not a universal kind. — س ره

They are one in nature and reality, but differ in how we consider them. Existence stated as a predicate lies outside the ten basic categories; the kind set against it is the category of relation. Relation is a second-order idea, and second-order ideas have a weak kind of realization. In that respect, they belong to the same broad nature as existence stated as a predicate. Consider this carefully; it is subtle. — ن ره
That is, the essences drawn from the different levels of existence as it unfolds. — ه ره

When linking existence is considered precisely as a link, it is not an existence or a thing in its own right. If we call it “existence” in this respect, the word is being used in a different sense; that is the correct account. But when the mind turns toward the link and makes a judgment about it or through it, it becomes existence stated as a predicate. The same happens with grammatical linking words: while they serve as links and tools, they are not complete, independent ideas; when we focus on them and make them the subject of a judgment, they become independent noun-like ideas. What is incomplete becomes complete; what is only potential becomes actual. There is a difference between being a thing and merely having the possibility of being one: possibility, just as possibility, is not a thing in its own right unless considered in another way. The author will explain this further when he discusses matter as an abstract mental idea. — ه ره

If their agreement were in some other meaning, that meaning would itself have to be predicated of them, and the distinction would collapse. Perhaps the author means that the difference between them is so great that they nearly share a word only, as in the earlier discussion of how essence is described as existing. Otherwise, this would conflict with what he has established throughout the book: abstract ideas, relations, and absences all have some share in existence. This view also answers a serious difficulty for philosophers who discuss second-order ideas and relational features even though philosophy is supposed to study real things. The author says that links and relations exist in the way relations exist, even if they do not exist as independent subjects. If they did not exist in this way, there would be no difference between true and false statements. Even if linking existence existed only in the mind, that would be enough, since existence has one nature whether it is mental or external, extremely strong or very weak. It is better to understand the author as speaking about how the two ideas differ when considered simply as ideas, and how the realities of linking and dependent existence differ—not as denying that the existences themselves share anything. In existence, what makes one thing distinct is also what it shares with others. The distinction is this: another relational existence attaches to the independent existence of whiteness once whiteness has been established as a real feature. First we establish, in a simple statement, that whiteness is real and belongs to the world outside the mind. Then we consider how whiteness is related to an ivory body, or how the body's existence is related to whiteness. Whether we express this connection by making whiteness or the body the subject of the statement depends on how the mind considers it. — س ره

Examples include blackness in a body or for a body; an effect's existence for its cause; and something known as present to the soul. As explained in The Clear Horizon, the point of this three-part division is that dependent existence is not limited to accidents. It also applies to forms present in matter, an effect's existence for its cause, the Active Intellect's existence for the soul, and God's existence for the world when discussing final causes. For us, the Active Intellect's presence to the soul is an example of existence “at” something; our perception of particular things is different, since the soul brings those perceptions about, so they are more like effects of a cause. A substance can be independent in relation to things below it, yet dependent in relation to God. In truth, every existence depends on God through a relation of manifestation, not through an ordinary relation between two separate things. The relation between the two kinds of linking existence is like the relation between real existence and an abstract idea. — س ره

This means existence in itself without being a feature, as with a substance; or existence in itself as a feature, as with an accident, when we consider it both in itself and as belonging to something else. Or the author may mean the three divisions explained earlier: existence in itself only, existence in itself and for itself, and existence in itself and through itself. — س ره
As in a compound statement describing something by a feature. — س ره
This is true according to the initial division, though the author will later say that nonexistence has no linking relation. — ط ره
“Linking nonexistence” here means the absence of a link. This is like using the words “categorical” or “conditional” for negative statements. — س ره

Philosophers divide necessity into many forms—essential, eternal, temporary, recurring, and others—but these reduce to three basic kinds. They are features of linking existence, meaning that one thing is affirmed of another. That is why the discussion of them follows the discussion of this kind of existence. — س ره
The opposite of necessity includes possibility and impossibility. — س ره
That is, necessity of existence or necessity of nonexistence, which includes both necessity and impossibility. — س ره

One answer is that possibility in the narrow sense means that both existence and nonexistence are possible. If broad possibility is already understood, the narrow sense needs no separate definition: we can simply say that it consists of two broad possibilities. The reason it needs a definition at all is that the broad sense is not yet understood. So defining it through impossibility still leaves a circle. — س ره

The flaw in the definition of possibility is that “impossible,” which appears in the definition, has not been explained. Its definition circles back to necessity, and the definition of necessity in turn depends on impossibility. — س ره

Otherwise, the definition would also apply to the First Effect, since its absence would entail the impossible absence of God. The author is concerned not only with whether the definition applies to the thing being defined, but also with whether it excludes other things. — س ره

One example is a circle between two conditions. Al-Khafrī argues that if we suppose the Necessary One does not exist, the nature of an existing thing depends on the nature of a maker, and the maker's nature depends on that existing thing. The author replies that a circle between two natures is not itself a problem; it is like the old puzzle about which came first, the egg or the chicken. Even if an impossibility followed, it would not be clearer than the assumption that God does not exist. That is different from the impossibility of God's nonexistence itself, which needs no further result to make it impossible. Just as every existence must ultimately depend on what is necessary in itself, every impossibility must ultimately depend on what is impossible in itself: God's nonexistence. — س ره

We will see that the possibility of dependent existences means their essential need: they are relations and connections in their very nature, not things that first exist on their own and then acquire a relation. Necessity is existence made firm; impossibility is nonexistence made firm. Possibility is the absence of both kinds of firmness: it is neither necessary existence nor necessary nonexistence, but lies between them. In this sense, possibility can be stronger or weaker depending on how near it is to either side. — ن ره

This division raises three problems. First, it seems to divide everything that exists into what exists through itself and what exists through something else, leaving no room to divide what is necessary into what is necessary in itself, through another, or in relation to another. Second, “existent” must be broad enough to include both what exists through itself and essences that exist through existence. And “drawing existence from something” must mean judging that it is independently existent, either through itself or through another. If it simply means finding something existent, the division applies equally to every case, including necessary and contingent existence. A clearer form would be: anything the mind judges to exist independently either exists through itself or through another. This also leaves out purely relational existence, which is not independent even when considered together with the things it relates. Including the relation and its two ends in the same division creates another problem. The division can be rescued by asking instead: is anything the mind describes as existent in any way dependent on something else, or not? The first is possible; the second is necessary. Third, as stated, the division really separates independent existence from relational existence. It does not explain how necessity and possibility function in statements, as the three modalities do. — ط
The phrase “we do not judge them” refers to essences considered only in themselves. — ه ره

That is, universal composite essences such as human being and horse. Even though we can understand what they are in themselves, once we set aside their defining concepts, we can no longer point to them as things. — س ره

The “causes” here are the causes included in a definition. As Avicenna says, the middle term is what we place after the word “because,” and it is the same in kind and reality as the final element in a definition: the thing's own nature. A defining feature is a thing's form, and a thing is what it is through its form. Avicenna says that a thing's form is its essence, the basis on which it is what it is. These three ways of speaking are close in meaning.

The account suited to philosophers who seek divine wisdom is this. Aristotle's claim that the answers to “What is it?” and “Why is it?” are often the same points to a subtle truth. The cause of a limited, particular existence, such as Zayd's, is the sacred outpouring of existence. The appearance of the limited thing is contained within the appearance of its source, as the lights of the stars are, in a certain respect, contained within the sun's light. Its reality is also that source, because the source brings it to completion; a thing is what it is through its completeness, not through its deficiency.

In The Beginning and the Return, the author says that, for careful thinkers in Aristotle’s school, the agent's causal role is included in what makes a thing existent. Elsewhere, he asks: if prime matter is nothing but pure potentiality, possibility, and vagueness, what distinguishes one prime matter from another? Some philosophers say that the heavenly spheres have their own prime matter, different from the matter of the elements. He replies that the different kinds of matter are distinguished by their causes. Their actual form comes from the nearest causes, the active intellects, which contribute to the material things along with the forms that enter them. He adds that one might say, by analysis, that a thing becomes definite through its proximate agent and so is determined by something outside it. But we must remember that an agent is like the thing's own reality—indeed, closer to it than it is to itself. So a thing's determination by its agent is not a determination by something outside its reality.

The point is that the actualization of forms is also the actualization of matter, and the differences among forms are the differences that make matter definite. If we ask what matter is in reality, we can answer: fire, air, and the other forms it takes on. Matter joined to what is continuous is continuous; joined to what is separate, it is separate; joined to water, it is water; joined to air, it is air. The form and its cause work together to make matter definite. In many things, the same is true of particular existences and the sacred outpouring: the source's manifestation is contained within theirs. Some mystics even use “matter” for this outpoured existence, reversing the usual philosophical account of matter and form. The author may also mean separate immaterial lights, which have no cause other than existence itself. For them, the answer to “What is it?” and “Why is it?” is the same, whether the cause is understood as what brings them about or as what they are directed toward. — س ره
A defining feature is the form of a thing, and its form is what makes it what it is. That is why “What is it?” and “Why is it?” can have the same answer. — ه ره

As stated at the beginning of the chapter, “real” has four meanings: a synonym for existence in general; lasting existence, as with an intellect or God; what is necessary in itself; and a statement or belief that matches what exists outside the mind. — س ره

The distinction is that reality means actual existence, and a statement is called “real” because what it says is actual. “Truth,” by contrast, means that the statement matches what exists outside the mind. — ط

If Zayd is standing in reality, then the statement “Zayd is standing” is true, and the reality itself is real. It is strained to say that the statement is “real” because of what it is about, as though we were describing something by a feature of its object. — س ره
The most basic truths in our ideas belong to existence simply as existence, since it is the clearest and most self-evident of all ideas. Our first true judgments depend on this. — س ره

The sophists must be answered before the main arguments begin: until their position is ruled out, proof has no force. There is a small ambiguity in Avicenna's wording. “Or do you doubt?” might mean “Do you know that you are doubting?” But then the later question, “Do you know that you doubted?” seems repetitive. It can also be read as the opposite of “Do you know?”; that reading has its own grammatical difficulty. Either way, the passage can be understood without repetition if the later question is taken as a branch of the first, or if we understand an unstated question about whether they know that they doubt. The word “deny” also suggests that doubt is followed by denial. In the first reading, “you doubted” and “you denied” are used as if the actions happened on their own, unlike the earlier, more direct wording. — س ره

The better answer is this: if by “necessary for the essences themselves” you mean that the feature belongs necessarily to the essence, we accept that implication and deny that the result is false. But if you mean that the feature is necessary because the essence it follows from is itself necessary, we deny that implication. — س ره
The reply here is made by al-Sayyid al-Sharif in his commentary on the earlier version of the book. — ه ره

That is, it does not follow that four must exist. One might expect the wording “evenness need not exist necessarily.” But if evenness existed necessarily, four would have to exist necessarily too: evenness cannot exist without what it belongs to, and it is a feature of quantity. That is why the author speaks of the number four. — س ره

As al-Lahiji says in The Dawning Lights, what seems to differ in this discipline is the predicate to which necessity is applied. Here the predicate is existence itself. The idea of necessity does not change; the discussion simply narrows it to one particular predicate. — ه ره

This is al-Dawani. His reasoning is that evenness belongs directly to the essence of four. It does not depend on a maker except indirectly, since possible things become actual only through creation. It does not depend on the existence of four in its own right either; when four is actual, its essence and its existence are together. The author is rejecting the mistaken idea that this makes an essence a combination of itself and an added existence, or turns the statement into one whose truth is conditional on the thing's existence. — س ره

The author distinguishes three things: eternal necessity in itself; necessity that holds while a thing exists, without being caused by its existence; and necessity that depends on a description or condition. The objector confused the second with the third, treating necessary features of an essence as conditional on its being created. The existence in “four is even while four exists” marks when the statement holds; it is not the reason evenness belongs to four. Nor should necessity while a thing exists be confused with God's eternal necessity. A feature can be necessary to its essence even if that essence is not necessary in itself; the statement itself is necessary in the essential sense. — س ره

Both claims are self-evident; the author's discussion draws attention to them. One consequence is that God must be simple: if He had parts that were each necessary, their combination would not make them one, since necessary beings could be related only by possibility. Each part would remain a separate simple being, contrary to what we have established. Another consequence is that there can be no endless chain of necessary beings. This will appear in the Illuminationist philosopher's proof that the Necessary One has no essence beyond His existence: if He had an essence, there would be infinitely many instances of it that were each necessary in themselves. We could not then reject them by saying that they form an endless chain, since none would be more basic than another. — س ره

When a statement is qualified by “insofar as” or “considered as,” the qualification can serve three purposes. First, it can mean that we consider the subject with everything else set aside; this is an unrestricted qualification. For example, “An essence considered just as an essence has this rule” means that we consider it without reference to anything else. In one later discussion, the author divides this unrestricted case into two. Second, the qualification can give the reason why the statement applies, as in “A human being laughs insofar as he is amazed.” Third, it can tell us to consider the subject and the qualification together, as in “A body, insofar as it is a surface, is white.” — س ره

The examples after “any further feature” list broad classes after more specific ones. The point is to exclude every added aspect, whether abstract or attached. “Zayd is possible” works as an example if possibility means that existence and nonexistence are equally open. If possibility means only that existence is not necessary, it belongs to the negative kind of qualification. More precisely, the list should mention explanatory and limiting conditions before features that are attached or abstracted, and should distinguish negative from positive and relational from nonrelational conditions. — س ره
One existence is through itself because it is necessary; the other is through another because of the necessary connection. — س ره
That is, one of the two existences is necessary in itself, and the other is necessary through it because of their connection. — ن ره

Or the point may be that the Necessary One is not caused by another necessary being. A possible effect of the Necessary One, though it does not bring about its own existence, still depends on and calls for that cause. — س ره

The kind of possibility that rules out necessity in itself is possibility in a thing's own nature. That does not rule out its being possible in relation to something else—unless the two are necessarily linked, which cannot be true of two necessary beings. — س ره

Sometimes a definition must repeat an idea in order to explain a relation. To know either of two related things, we have to know the other; they are equally familiar or unfamiliar. Yet a definition is supposed to start from what is already known. So we must mention the cause that makes them related, so that both can be understood at once, while directing the definition to whichever one we mean to define. Consider Avicenna's definition of a father: “An animal who brings forth another of his kind from his seed, insofar as he is such.” “Animal” and “another of his kind” name the father and son without yet mentioning their relation. “Brings forth from his seed” gives the cause of their relation. “Insofar as he is such” repeats part of what has already been said, but the repetition is necessary: it makes the relation belong to the animal specifically as a father. Otherwise the definition could apply to an animal who is a father in some other respect, even though the aim is to define what makes him a father. — س ره

The first wording is “His own reality is His existence.” The second says that He has no essence apart from His existence. The first already conveys the second, especially after the author explains that He has no separate essence, but it fits the Ashʿarite position more closely, as al-Lahiji notes in The Dawning Lights. — س ره

This discussion is needed even if we divide existents into what the mind recognizes as existing through itself and what it recognizes as existing through something else. A possible thing might exist through an intermediary in what makes it real, as a dependent existence does, or through an intermediary in how it is described, as an essence does. The Necessary One exists through Himself, without an external intermediary of either kind. Still, the proofs for God's existence establish that nothing stands between Him and the fact that He exists; this discussion is needed to show that nothing stands between Him and the judgment that He exists, and so to complete the division. — ط

By “the thing exists before its existence,” we mean that its essence would be prior through its own existence. This makes the contradiction immediate; the author is not relying on the proof in The Discussions that the claim leads to an endless series. If a thing could be prior to itself, it would also be prior to what is prior to it—again, itself—and the sequence would continue. Saying that it would “exist twice” is only a brief way of making the point. The sentence about whether the prior existence is the essence or something else is not needed to show that a thing cannot exist before itself; this contradiction is far clearer than an endless series. How could the less obvious problem prove the more obvious one? The series could instead be used as an additional argument against self-priority, which would make that sentence relevant. “Essence” here can mean any essence, not only God's. — س ره

You might ask: how can existence be necessary in itself if it is made necessary by the essence? If existence were necessary through itself, it would not depend on the essence. And at the level of the essence itself, that essence is neither existence nor existent. I reply: that is what you mean by necessity in itself. For someone who holds that the Necessary Being has an essence, being necessary in itself means that the essence itself requires its own existence, with no help from anything else. This thinker also holds that existence is not found at the level of the essence considered in itself. To argue against that view by assuming the opposite is to assume what needs to be proved. — س ره

It would be better to call this priority a priority in what a thing is. When we consider an essence in itself, we set aside both existence and nonexistence. We are not comparing two things that already exist. Its defining part comes before the whole, and the essence comes before what necessarily follows from it. Even if essences were established separately from every kind of existence—as the Muʿtazilites held—this priority would remain. Both what comes first and the respect in which it comes first belong to what the thing is. — س ره

“Thing” here explains the word “essence,” as in the saying that the names for kinds of thing are familiar while the names for kinds of existence are not. Thinghood and existence are two ways of speaking about the same reality. Avicenna's point is that a cause and its effect must be alike in the relevant respect. — س ره
As the essence of four is the cause of the essence of evenness. — س ره
This may be a quotation from Avicenna, though I do not have a copy of The Book of Discussions to check. — س ره

That is, suppose someone says that a cause and effect must exist together: if the cause exists, the effect exists; if the cause does not exist, neither does the effect. The reply is that the essence is not thereby the cause of existence. What follows from an essence as such follows in every condition, so it could follow even when the essence does not exist, as explained earlier. — س ره

Beyond supporting the high claim that the Necessary One is pure existence, Avicenna's passage directly affirms that existence itself is real and has primacy. This is the central point here and in many other major questions. — س ره

This contrast applies when a general kind and distinguishing feature are considered as such. If they are taken as mental matter and form, they are two things: the matter can be complete before receiving this form, and once it receives the form they unite without distinction. A form can also become separate and exist in the world of images or among the intellects, without matter. The author explains this elsewhere. — س ره

Someone might object that the author himself often recognizes other kinds of priority, including priority by essence and by what is more entitled to something, and that these would support the objection. The answer is that he is speaking here in the familiar language of other philosophers, not giving his own final account. — س ره
The argument rules out real, external existence as a necessary feature of essence. The general idea “existent,” by contrast, can be applied to an essence at any level we consider it. — ط

The sound answer, I think, is that existence does not have existence as an added feature that needs a cause. Saying instead that existence causes its own being-existent without a second existence does not remove the difficulty. For what does “being existent” mean? If it means actual existence, to put existence before its being-existent is to put a thing before itself. If it means the concept of being existent, such priority is not impossible—but neither is it impossible for something other than existence to come before that concept.

One might escape the difficulty by taking “existence” to mean the level of divine oneness, the hidden treasure, and “being existent” to mean the level of manifestation, being known, and the outpouring of existence. We will later discuss a further kind of priority, priority in truth. But that does not fit the approach of the thinker who presents this argument, the author of The Adjudications.

Again, perhaps in saying that the same objection applies to existence, he means the concept of existence. But that concept is itself among the essences and needs real existence. He cannot then say that the essence of existence precedes its being-existent through itself: the concept counts as “existence” only in the primary sense in which a meaning is predicated of itself, not as an independently existing reality. — س ره
